bandsNote: Hidden from students. Band 1 starts the Checks tab and rises only by clean first tries. The top band IS the regular-level standard: no AP content, nothing labeled extension, challenge or optional.
standard: T5 (the standard every student completes): state in words, with numbers from your own tables, how acceleration changes when the fan force doubles and when the mass doubles.
hintRule: Hint 1 points to the step card. Hint 2 does the first step. Hint 3 shows the same move on another example. No hint gives the answer. Each hint costs a fresh attempt.
tolerance: num items accept the answer plus or minus tol (m/s2); ratio answers are from the doubling rule, so tol covers the tiny drag in the data

items.prompt: Two carts start at rest. Speed graph A reaches 1.2 m/s after 2.0 s. Speed graph B reaches 0.6 m/s after 2.0 s. Which cart has the bigger acceleration?
hints: Open your step card, step 4. Acceleration is how much the speed grows each second.
First step: find how much the speed of cart A grew. It started at 0 and reached 1.2 m/s.
Same move on another pair: one cart grows 0.4 m/s in 2.0 s and another grows 0.8 m/s in 2.0 s. The second one gains more every second, so it has the bigger acceleration.
items.misc: Students compare the final speeds without noticing both carts took the same time, or pick the cart whose line starts higher.

items.prompt: A cart's speed grows from 0 to 1.20 m/s in 2.0 s. What is its acceleration?
hints: Open your step card, step 4. The markers read speed gained per second.
First step: the speed gained is 1.20 − 0 = 1.20 m/s. Next, divide by the time.
Same move on another cart: speed grows from 0 to 0.90 m/s in 3.0 s. Gained 0.90 m/s. Divide by 3.0 s. Acceleration 0.30 m/s².
items.misc: Students give the final speed as the acceleration, or multiply by the time instead of dividing.

items.prompt: A 1.00 kg cart is run at fan force 0.15 N and then at 0.30 N. The acceleration goes from 0.14 to 0.29 m/s². About how many times bigger is the acceleration?
hints: Open your step card, step 6. Compare the acceleration at two fan settings.
First step: divide the new acceleration by the old one: 0.29 ÷ 0.14.
Same move on another pair: force 0.10 N gave 0.10 m/s² and force 0.30 N gave 0.31 m/s². 0.31 ÷ 0.10 is about 3 times.
items.misc: Students say the acceleration went up by 0.15, the same as the force, instead of comparing how many times bigger.

items.prompt: The fan force stays at 0.45 N. The mass goes from 0.50 kg to 1.00 kg. The acceleration goes from 0.88 to 0.44 m/s². What happened to the acceleration when the mass doubled?
hints: Open your step card, step 8. Compare the acceleration at two masses.
First step: divide the new acceleration by the old one: 0.44 ÷ 0.88.
Same move on another pair: mass 1.0 kg gave 0.60 m/s² and mass 3.0 kg gave 0.20 m/s². 0.20 ÷ 0.60 is about one third.
items.misc: Students expect more mass to give more acceleration, the same way more force does.

items.prompt: A fan force of 0.15 N gave a 1.00 kg cart 0.14 m/s². A force of 0.30 N gave it 0.29 m/s². Predict the acceleration for a force of 0.60 N.
hints: Open your step card, step 6. Each time the force doubles, so does the acceleration.
First step: how many times bigger is 0.60 N than 0.30 N?
Same move: 0.10 N gave 0.20 m/s². Predict 0.30 N. It is 3 times the force, so 3 × 0.20 = 0.60 m/s².
items.misc: Students add 0.30 to the acceleration instead of scaling it.

items.prompt: The fan force stays the same. A 0.75 kg cart accelerates at 0.59 m/s². Predict the acceleration of a 1.50 kg cart.
hints: Open your step card, step 8. Each time the mass doubles, the acceleration is cut in half.
First step: how many times bigger is 1.50 kg than 0.75 kg?
Same move: a 0.40 kg cart gave 0.80 m/s². Predict 0.80 kg. It is 2 times the mass, so half the acceleration: 0.40 m/s².
items.misc: Students double the acceleration because the mass doubled.

items.prompt: Part 1: acceleration on the up axis, fan force across, mass fixed. Which picture shows the shape of your data?
options: rising straight line from near the corner
hints: Open your step card, step 8. Graph acceleration against fan force.
First step: plot the first two points: (0.15, 0.14) and (0.30, 0.29). Did the point go up or down?
Same move: points (1, 2) and (2, 4) go up, and the next point (3, 6) keeps going up in a straight line.
items.misc: Students draw a curve through points that lie on a line.

items.prompt: Part 2: acceleration on the up axis, mass across, fan force fixed. Which picture shows the shape of your data?
hints: Open your step card, step 8. Graph acceleration against mass.
First step: plot the first two points: (0.50, 0.88) and (0.75, 0.59). Did the point go up or down, and by how much?
Same move: points (1.0, 0.60) and (2.0, 0.30) and (3.0, 0.20) fall fast and then slowly.
items.misc: Students draw a straight falling line because the first two points look straight.

items.prompt: A 1.00 kg cart at 0.30 N accelerates at 0.29 m/s². A stronger fan makes the force 0.60 N and the cart is loaded to 2.00 kg. Predict the new acceleration.
hints: Open your step card, steps 6 and 8. Change one thing at a time.
First step: double the force alone. What happens to the acceleration?
Same move: a = 0.20 m/s². Force triples, then mass triples. Tripling the force triples a to 0.60. Tripling the mass cuts it by 3 to 0.20 again.
items.misc: Students double the acceleration for the force and forget the mass, or add the two changes.

items.prompt: Which sentence do the Part 1 and Part 2 data support?
options: Doubling the fan force about doubles the acceleration, and doubling the mass about halves it.
Doubling the fan force about halves the acceleration, and doubling the mass about doubles it.
Doubling the fan force about doubles the acceleration, and doubling the mass changes nothing.
Doubling the fan force or doubling the mass about doubles the acceleration.
hints: Open your step card, step 9. Your claim must match the numbers in your table.
First step: in your table, find two rows where only the force changed. What did the acceleration do?
Same move on another table: force 0.10 N gave 0.20 m/s² and force 0.20 N gave 0.40 m/s². Only the force changed, and a doubled.

items.prompt: The fan force stays at 0.45 N. A 0.50 kg cart accelerated at 0.88 m/s² and a 1.00 kg cart at 0.44 m/s². Predict the acceleration of a 2.00 kg cart.
hints: Open your step card, step 8. Compare the mass to a mass you already ran.
First step: how many times bigger is 2.00 kg than 1.00 kg?
Same move: 0.30 kg gave 1.20 m/s². Predict 0.90 kg. It is 3 times the mass, so one third the acceleration: 0.40 m/s².
items.misc: Students halve from the 0.50 kg value instead of the 1.00 kg value, or subtract.

items.prompt: A student says: "The fan force was the same 0.45 N for the 0.50 kg cart and the 1.50 kg cart, so their accelerations should match." What do the data say?
options: The 1.50 kg cart had about one third the acceleration (0.29 versus 0.88 m/s²), so the same force does not give the same acceleration.
The student is right: the same force gives the same acceleration.
The 1.50 kg cart had about three times the acceleration.
The 1.50 kg cart had about half the acceleration.
hints: Open your step card, step 8. Look up both masses in your Part 2 table.
First step: find the acceleration of the 0.50 kg cart and of the 1.50 kg cart in your table.
Same move: a 0.20 kg cart had 1.50 m/s² and a 0.60 kg cart had 0.50 m/s². The heavier cart had a third of the acceleration, so the same force does not match.
items.misc: Students think equal force means equal motion.
